UIKit is Apple's imperative UI framework for iOS, iPadOS, tvOS and Catalyst — it has powered every iOS app since 2008. Core types include `UIView`, `UIViewController`, `UIWindow`, `UINavigationController`, `UITableView`, `UICollectionView`.

### In modern apps
- Greenfield iOS apps often start with SwiftUI; UIKit is reached for when SwiftUI lacks features (custom transitions, certain gestures, complex collections).
- You can mix the two: `UIHostingController` hosts SwiftUI inside UIKit; `UIViewRepresentable` / `UIViewControllerRepresentable` hosts UIKit inside SwiftUI.
- UIKit still backs all third-party iOS code shipped before iOS 13 and remains the default in many enterprise codebases.

Only `viewDidLoad` fires once per controller instance; the appear and disappear callbacks fire again every single time the screen comes back.

- `init(nibName:bundle:)` / `init(coder:)` — the controller exists, its view does not. Touching `view` here forces it to load early.
- `loadView()` — the root view is being created. Override only when you build the hierarchy in code and want to replace the root view outright; never call `super` there if you assign your own.
- `viewDidLoad()` — the view is in memory. One-time setup: subviews, constraints, cell registration, delegates.
- `viewWillAppear(_:)` — about to become visible, on every appearance. Refresh data that may have changed while you were away, add observers.
- `viewDidAppear(_:)` — on screen and the transition is finished. Start animations, fire the screen-view analytics event, kick off work you deferred.
- `viewWillDisappear(_:)` / `viewDidDisappear(_:)` — leaving. Save drafts, pause timers and video, remove observers you added on appear.
- `viewWillLayoutSubviews()` / `viewDidLayoutSubviews()` — the layout pass. These run many times per appearance, so keep them cheap and idempotent.
- `deinit` — deallocated. Invalidate timers and cancel long-running tasks.

The follow-up interviewers reach for: heavy work in `viewWillAppear` stutters the push animation, because the transition has not started yet. Move it to `viewDidAppear` or into a cancellable task.

A view's frame is measured in its superview's coordinate system, its bounds is the view's own coordinate system, and that difference is exactly what makes scrolling work.

- `frame` — where I sit inside my superview and how big I am.
- `bounds` — my internal coordinate space. The origin is normally (0,0) and the size matches the view. Moving `bounds.origin` changes which part of myself is on screen, which is how UIScrollView scrolls: `contentOffset` is `bounds.origin`.
- `center` — my midpoint in superview coordinates. Setting it moves the frame and leaves bounds untouched.

Once the view carries a non-identity `transform` — rotation, scale — `frame` is only the axis-aligned bounding box of the transformed view, so setting it is meaningless. Position with `center`, size with `bounds`, and rotate or scale with `transform`.

A subview's frame is expressed in its parent's bounds, so changing the parent's `bounds.origin` moves every child on screen without touching a single child frame.

Every touch is resolved in two passes: UIKit first hit-tests to find the view under the finger, then delivers the event up the responder chain starting from that view.

1. Hit-testing — beginning at the window, UIKit calls `hitTest(_:with:)` recursively; each view answers `point(inside:with:)` and the deepest subview containing the point wins. Views that are hidden, have an alpha below 0.01, or have `isUserInteractionEnabled == false` are skipped entirely, and hit-testing never escapes a superview's bounds — which is why a button poking outside its parent is untappable.
2. Delivery — `touchesBegan/Moved/Ended/Cancelled` is sent to the hit view. If it does not implement them, or implements them and calls `super`, the event walks up the responder chain: view → superview → … → view controller → its parent controller → window → application.

Gesture recognizers attached to the hit view or to any ancestor see the touches first and can cancel delivery to the view, which is why adding a plain tap recognizer to a container quietly breaks a table view's row selection underneath.

`UIResponder` is the shared superclass of UIView, UIViewController, UIWindow and UIApplication, so the same chain also carries motion events, key commands and target-less `sendAction` calls. First responder status is a separate idea: it names the responder that receives keyboard input, not the one that received the touch.

Both are scroll-based containers backed by a data source and a delegate.

- Data source supplies cells (and, for collections, supplementary views) for index paths.
- Delegate notifies about selection, sizing, scroll, etc.
- **Cell reuse** — instead of creating thousands of cells, the view recycles offscreen cells via `dequeueReusableCell(withIdentifier:for:)`. Cells must implement `prepareForReuse()` to wipe state.
- **Modern API**: UITableViewDiffableDataSource / UICollectionViewDiffableDataSource — declare snapshots of (Section, Item), the framework computes the diff and animates inserts/deletes/moves automatically.
- Compositional layout (UICollectionViewCompositionalLayout) — describe complex grids/lists as composable sections.

Storyboards, XIBs and code are three ways to build the same UIKit screen, and they differ mainly in how well they survive a team, a merge and a refactor.

- **Storyboards** — a visual editor for whole flows, with segues between scenes. Fast to prototype and easy to show a designer; painful to merge because the XML is machine-generated, slow to open once large, and a lot of behaviour hides in inspector checkboxes that no code review will ever catch.
- **XIBs** — one view or one screen per nib. The same visual benefit with a much smaller blast radius, and a reasonable fit for reusable custom views.
- **Programmatic** — the view tree built in Swift. Reviewable diffs, easy to parameterise and refactor, no runtime string identifiers; more typing, and no canvas unless you wrap the view in a SwiftUI `#Preview`.

Teams of any size have largely converged on programmatic UIKit or SwiftUI for new screens. Storyboards survive mostly as the launch screen, and even that is now better expressed as the `UILaunchScreen` dictionary in Info.plist.

The signal an interviewer is listening for is the merge argument, not a stylistic preference.

AppDelegate owns process-level events, while each UI instance is a `UIWindowScene` whose SceneDelegate owns the window and the foreground and background transitions.

### AppDelegate
- `application(_:didFinishLaunchingWithOptions:)` — runs once per process. Build the dependency graph, start analytics, register for push. Keep it short; every millisecond here is launch time.
- `application(_:configurationForConnecting:options:)` — the system asks which scene configuration to use when a new window connects.
- Remote notification and background-fetch callbacks, plus `applicationWillTerminate`, which is not called for a suspended app and must never be your only save point.

### SceneDelegate
- `scene(_:willConnectTo:options:)` — create the `UIWindow` for that scene, set the root view controller, and handle a URL, shortcut or user activity that launched it.
- `sceneDidBecomeActive` / `sceneWillResignActive` — start and pause anything that should not run while a call or the app switcher is on screen.
- `sceneWillEnterForeground` / `sceneDidEnterBackground` — refresh on the way in; save state and stop timers on the way out.

The states are not running, inactive, active, background and suspended. Backgrounding gives you seconds: use `beginBackgroundTask` to finish something small, and `BGTaskScheduler` for anything real.

Because iPad and Mac can run several scenes at once, anything scene-scoped — the window, the root controller, the currently displayed document — must not be a singleton on AppDelegate. A SwiftUI app expresses the same thing with the `App` protocol, a `WindowGroup` and the `scenePhase` environment value, and reaches for `@UIApplicationDelegateAdaptor` when it still needs the delegate callbacks.

The view handles touches, layout and the responder chain, while the layer it owns holds the bitmap that is actually drawn and animated.

- A view is its layer's delegate, and almost every visual property you set — `backgroundColor`, `cornerRadius`, `shadowOpacity`, `mask` — is really a layer property. Layers are cheap because they carry no event handling; views are the expensive ones.
- `UIView.animate` works by installing Core Animation animations on the layer, so animation was always a layer feature.
- A standalone layer animates its properties implicitly over a quarter of a second. A layer backing a view does not, because the view disables those default actions. `CATransaction` is how you re-enable or suppress them.
- During an animation the model layer already holds the final value, so `frame` and hit-testing report the destination, not what you see. `layer.presentation()` gives the on-screen values — the standard answer to "why is my animating button not tappable where it looks".

### When to reach for a layer directly
- A gradient, a shape, a replicator, an emitter, tiled content or a video surface — `CAGradientLayer`, `CAShapeLayer`, `CAEmitterLayer`, `AVPlayerLayer`. Overriding `layerClass` makes the view's own backing layer that type, which keeps it in sync with layout for free.
- Animating something UIKit has no property for: `strokeEnd`, `path`, `shadowPath`, or a 3D transform with perspective.
- **Performance work**: an explicit `shadowPath`, `shouldRasterize` for static content, and `contentsScale` when you draw manually.

What you give up is everything the view provides — no touch handling, no Auto Layout, no accessibility — so a layer is for pixels, not for controls.

Pushing adds a controller to an existing navigation stack, presenting puts one on top modally regardless of any stack, and containment makes one controller a child that lives inside your own view.

- **Push** — `navigationController?.pushViewController(vc, animated: true)`. You get the back button, the interactive pop gesture and the title bar. `setViewControllers(_:animated:)` rewrites the whole stack, which is how deep links land several screens in at once.
- **Present** — `present(vc, animated: true)`. The default style is a sheet, and `sheetPresentationController` gives you detents, a grabber and dismissal behaviour. `dismiss` is handled by the presenting controller; calling it on the presented one forwards up, which is why it works either way.
- **Containment** — `addChild(child)`, add `child.view` and constrain it, then `child.didMove(toParent: self)`. Removing is the mirror image, starting with `willMove(toParent: nil)`. Skipping those calls leaves a controller whose appearance callbacks, trait propagation and rotation handling are silently broken.

Containment is how you build a custom container — a pager, a card stack, a screen that swaps between empty, loading and content — and how you cut a huge view controller into reusable pieces without inventing a new architecture.

One lifecycle detail interviewers like: a full-screen presentation calls `viewWillDisappear` on the presenter, but a `.pageSheet` does not, because the presenter is still visible behind it. Any refresh logic living in `viewWillAppear` will not run when that sheet is dismissed.

A delegate is a one-to-one callback contract, and the property is `weak` because the delegate almost always owns the object it delegates for — a strong reference back would close a retain cycle and leak both.

- A view controller owns its table view, and the table view's `delegate` points at the controller. If that pointer were strong, neither would ever deallocate.
- `weak` requires a class-bound protocol, so delegate protocols are declared `: AnyObject`. A struct cannot be a weak delegate.
- The naming convention passes the sender as the first argument — `tableView(_:didSelectRowAt:)` — so one object can act as delegate for several senders and still tell them apart.
- For methods that should be optional, prefer a default implementation in a protocol extension over `@objc optional`, which drags the whole thing into the Objective-C runtime.

When a closure is the better fit: a single callback, no shared identity, and the caller wants to capture context. The cost is that the closure is stored strongly, so `[weak self]` becomes your problem instead.

When a notification is the better fit: genuinely one-to-many, with observers that the sender should know nothing about — keyboard frames, app lifecycle, a logout that several screens react to. The cost is no compile-time contract and no easy way to trace who reacts.

Modern code often replaces all three: `async`/`await` for a one-shot result, `AsyncStream` or Combine for a sequence of events, and in SwiftUI, closures and bindings. Delegation still earns its place where the callbacks are many, named, and worth mocking in a test.

Animating a constraint means changing its `constant` and then calling `layoutIfNeeded()` inside the animation block, because it is the layout pass — not the assignment — that gets animated.

### The APIs, in the order you should think of them
- `UIView.animate(withDuration:...)` — the workhorse for alpha, transform, colours and layout passes. The newer `UIView.animate(springDuration:bounce:)` describes a spring by feel instead of by damping ratios.
- `UIViewPropertyAnimator` — the same animations, but pausable, reversible and scrubbable through `fractionComplete`. This is what gesture-driven interactions and interactive dismissals are built on.
- `UIView.transition(with:duration:options:)` — for changes that are not animatable properties at all. `isHidden`, `text` and `image` do not interpolate, so you cross-dissolve the view instead.
- **Core Animation** — `CABasicAnimation` and friends for layer-only properties such as `strokeEnd`, `path` and `shadowPath`.

### Two habits save most of the debugging
- Prefer `transform` over `frame` for movement and scaling. It skips the layout pass and composites on the GPU, and Auto Layout will not overwrite it on the next pass — an animated frame under Auto Layout snaps back the moment anything triggers layout.
- Call `layoutIfNeeded()` once before the block to flush pending changes, so the animation starts from a settled state rather than interpolating from a half-applied layout.

`UIViewRepresentable` wraps a UIKit view so SwiftUI can use it, and `UIHostingController` wraps a SwiftUI view so UIKit can use it.

### Going into SwiftUI
- `makeUIView(context:)` runs once and builds the view. `updateUIView(_:context:)` runs on every SwiftUI state change and must be idempotent — an unconditional write is how you get a text field whose cursor jumps to the end on every keystroke, so compare before assigning.
- `makeCoordinator()` supplies the object that holds delegate and target-action conformances, plus the `Binding`s that carry values back out. That is the whole of the UIKit-to-SwiftUI direction.
- A representable has no intrinsic size unless the wrapped view provides one. Implement `sizeThatFits(_:uiView:context:)`, or set hugging and compression priorities, or it will swallow the layout.
- `UIViewControllerRepresentable` does the same for whole controllers — photo pickers, mail composers, players.

### Going into UIKit
- `UIHostingController` is a normal view controller: install it with `addChild` / `didMove(toParent:)`. Setting `sizingOptions = [.intrinsicContentSize]` lets Auto Layout size it from the SwiftUI content.
- `UIHostingConfiguration` puts SwiftUI straight into a cell with no controller at all.
- The environment does not cross the boundary by itself. Inject what the SwiftUI side needs on `rootView` explicitly, and remember a UIKit navigation bar and a SwiftUI `NavigationStack` will fight over the title if you nest them.

Each crossing adds a hosting layer with its own layout and update cycle, so use a few deliberate boundaries rather than alternating frameworks at every level of the tree.
